hero.headline: Three-vehicle crash injures seven, closes northbound I-95 in Martin County
hero.teaser: All northbound lanes of I-95 are closed at mile marker 105 in Martin County after a three-vehicle crash injured seven people, according to the Martin County Sheriff’s Office. The c
hero.body:
All northbound lanes of I-95 are closed at mile marker 105 in Martin County after a three-vehicle crash injured seven people, according to the Martin County Sheriff’s Office. The crash site is roughly three miles north of High Meadow Avenue.

 The seven people have non-life-threatening injuries and are being transported to nearby hospitals, the sheriff’s office said.

 FHP will investigate the crash. The sheriff’s office said all northbound lanes are expected to stay closed for some time.

cards.headline: Student swims from school bus in Port St. Lucie floodwater, raising safety questions
cards.teaser: A student entered deep floodwater after leaving a school bus in Port St. Lucie on Monday, prompting parents to question St. Lucie Public Schools’ decisions to open schools during s
cards.body:
A student entered deep floodwater after leaving a school bus in Port St. Lucie on Monday, prompting parents to question St. Lucie Public Schools’ decisions to open schools during severe weather and send buses into flooded streets. A viral video shows the student swimming home through the neighborhood, where the water has since receded.

 Neighbor Ariel Abel said the bus became stuck before the student stepped into the water. “We watched the school bus get stuck over in that turn area, and then we watched the kid get off, and he sunk straight into the water.” Lucinda Lopez also described the danger: “He literally almost went completely underwater,” she said.

 Parents have questioned whether students should have sheltered at school until conditions improved rather than boarding buses traveling through severely flooded streets. The county’s first flood advisory came just after 8 a.m. Monday, and the first flash flood warning was issued at 10:41 a.m. “Seeing the danger that all of the kids were put in is not okay,” Lopez said.

 St. Lucie Public Schools Superintendent Dr. Jon Prince apologized to families for the district’s response during a news conference Tuesday. “I completely understand the frustration families feel,” Prince said. “It caused a lot of stress for our families, and for that, I’m profoundly sorry.”

 Some parents remained dissatisfied with the apology and called for changes to protect students. “An apology doesn’t fix what is happening,” Abel said. Lopez emphasized safety over attendance: “We need to do better. We need to protect our kids at all costs. Missing a day or two of school is okay if it means keeping our kids safe at all costs.”

cards.headline: Port St. Lucie dialysis patient recalls canal rescue as body-camera video is released
cards.teaser: Maria Andrade-Vasquez feared she would not survive when floodwaters swept her transport van into a canal. Body-camera video released this week shows the response that brought her and the driver to safety.
cards.body:
Maria Andrade-Vasquez feared she would not survive when floodwaters swept her dialysis transport van into a Port St. Lucie canal Monday. Now recovering at home, she is recounting the rescue as police body-camera video released this week shows how an officer and firefighters helped save her. “Yes, very, very scared,” Andrade-Vasquez said, speaking through her son, Raul Morales, who translated from Spanish.

 Andrade-Vasquez was riding home from treatment when the van was swept off the road near Lakehurst Drive in the Swan Park community. Police said Officer Peterson arrived just 100 seconds after being dispatched to reports of a transport van in a canal off Southwest Hogan Street. The video shows Peterson rushing into the water and rescuing the driver before learning that Andrade-Vasquez was still trapped inside. As water surrounded the vehicle, rescuers said, the van tilted into the canal, leaving her trapped in the back.

 Police Chief Leo Niemczyk said wheelchair equipment in the van blocked Andrade-Vasquez’s escape. “She's wheelchair bound, so the equipment that came out of the back of the van was up in place blocking her in,” Niemczyk said. “They had to get her out of the wheelchair and pull her up over the equipment to get her out of the van.” Firefighters with St. Lucie County Fire District joined Peterson and worked with him to free her, according to police. Both Andrade-Vasquez and the driver were rescued safely.

 Morales said his mother still struggles to understand how rescuers freed her so quickly. “To me it was amazing to see how quick they did what they did,” he said. Andrade-Vasquez, a mother of four, grandmother of 10 and cancer survivor, remains grateful to the first responders who saved her. Morales said she is still processing the trauma of the rescue and plans to continue dialysis treatments three times a week as she recovers at home with her family.

cards.headline: Looking for something to do this weekend? Here are the Top 5 local events for Nov. 6-8
cards.teaser: A Friday art walk in Stuart, the Navy SEAL Museum Muster in Fort Pierce, a Caribbean festival in Port St. Lucie, live music in Vero Beach and a downtown sidewalk sale lead the weekend.
cards.body:
The Treasure Coast has a busy first full weekend of November ahead, with an art walk in Stuart on Friday evening, a day celebrating Naval Special Warfare history in Fort Pierce on Saturday, Caribbean food and music in Port St. Lucie, live British Invasion favorites in Vero Beach and a downtown shopping event stretching into Sunday.

 Here are five standout events for Friday evening, Nov. 6, through Sunday, Nov. 8 , across Martin, St. Lucie and Indian River counties.

 1. First Friday Art Walk, Stuart

 When: Friday, Nov. 6, 5–9 p.m. Where: The Creek District of Arts & Entertainment, Stuart. Admission: No general admission price is listed; purchases at participating businesses are separate.

 The Creek District kicks off the weekend with its First Friday Art Walk, inviting visitors to spend the evening exploring the downtown arts neighborhood. The event brings together the district's galleries, businesses and creative community, giving residents an opportunity to discover local art while making an evening of downtown Stuart.

 For visitors who want a walkable Friday night outing, the art walk is a chance to browse, meet local creatives and stop at neighborhood shops or restaurants along the way. First Friday Art Walk details .

 2. 41st Annual Navy SEAL Museum Muster, Fort Pierce

 When: Saturday, Nov. 7, 8 a.m.–5 p.m. Where: Navy UDT-SEAL Museum, 3300 N. Highway A1A, Fort Pierce. Admission: Check the museum for admission and registration details; the related beach challenge has separate participation arrangements.

 The Navy SEAL Museum's 41st annual Muster returns to North Hutchinson Island for a day celebrating the history, traditions and service of the SEAL Teams. The museum's listing describes a reimagined event featuring its Muster Legacy Compound, leadership speakers and opportunities to connect with the Naval Special Warfare community.

 The weekend also includes the 22nd annual Navy SEAL Museum 5K Beach Challenge on Saturday morning. For families, military-history enthusiasts and visitors interested in the Treasure Coast's connection to Naval Special Warfare, the Muster offers one of the weekend's most distinctive outings. Muster information .

 3. Treasure Coast Caribbean Food & Music Festival, Port St. Lucie

 When: Saturday, Nov. 7, 2–10 p.m. Where: MIDFLORIDA Credit Union Event Center, 9221 SE Event Center Place, Port St. Lucie. Admission: Check the organizer for current ticket information.

 The Treasure Coast Caribbean Food & Music Festival fills Saturday afternoon and evening with Caribbean food, live entertainment, music and cultural activities. The family-oriented festival highlights the region's Caribbean community with participating vendors and performances.

 With an eight-hour schedule, visitors can make a full outing of the event or stop by later in the day for food and music. Festival details .

 4. St. Johns Wood at Riverside Theatre, Vero Beach

 When: Saturday, Nov. 7, 5:30–8:30 p.m. Where: Riverside Theatre, 3250 Riverside Park Drive, Vero Beach. Admission: Check the venue for seating and any applicable charges.

 Looking for live music in Indian River County? St. Johns Wood performs at Riverside Theatre on Saturday evening as part of the venue's Loop Music Calendar. The band plays British Invasion music from the 1960s and 1970s, offering a nostalgic soundtrack for fans of that era.

 The early-evening set makes this an option for anyone who wants to enjoy music without committing to a late night. St. Johns Wood performance details .

 5. Shopapalooza Fall Sidewalk Sale, Stuart

 When: Saturday and Sunday, Nov. 7–8, 10 a.m.–5 p.m. each day. Where: Downtown Stuart, along Osceola Street and participating downtown businesses. Admission: Free to browse; purchases are additional.

 Downtown Stuart's Shopapalooza Fall Sidewalk Sale gives shoppers two days to browse local merchants and look for seasonal finds. The event extends beyond a single afternoon, so visitors can make it a Saturday stop or save it for a more relaxed Sunday outing.

 It's also an opportunity to support downtown businesses while exploring the shops and restaurants around Osceola Street. Saturday details and Sunday details .

 Event times, prices and participation details can change. Check the linked organizers for the latest information before heading out. For more activities throughout Martin, St. Lucie and Indian River counties, explore the Treasure Coast Today events calendar .

hero.headline: Florida's Roof Age Law: The Roof Inspection Treasure Coast Homeowners Can Request Before Replacing a Roof Over 15 Years Old
hero.teaser: Under Florida Statute 627.7011, a homeowner with a roof 15 years or older can have it inspected before an insurer requires replacement. Here is what Martin and St. Lucie County homeowners should know, and what a proper roof inspection documents.
hero.body:
If you own a home in Stuart, Jensen Beach, Palm City, Port St. Lucie, Fort Pierce or anywhere along Hutchinson Island, and your roof is more than 15 years old, there is a good chance you have already received the letter. It says your homeowners insurance will not be renewed unless the roof is replaced. Many Treasure Coast homeowners assume they have two choices: pay for a new roof or lose coverage. Florida law gives them a third option, and most have never heard of it.

 What Florida's Roof Age Law Actually Says

 Florida Statute 627.7011(5), often called the Florida roof age law or the 15-year roof rule, applies to homeowners insurance policies issued or renewed on or after July 1, 2022. For a roof under 15 years old, an insurer may not refuse to issue or renew a policy solely because of the roof's age. For a roof 15 years or older, the insurer must allow the homeowner to have the roof inspected by an authorized inspector, at the homeowner's expense, before requiring replacement as a condition of coverage. If that roof inspection shows the roof has five or more years of remaining useful life, the insurer may not refuse to issue or renew the policy solely because of roof age.

 Authorized inspectors under the statute include Florida-licensed roofing contractors, home inspectors, building code inspectors, general or residential contractors, engineers and architects. The law applies to homeowners policies; it does not apply to a condominium association's master policy, and it does not override every other underwriting decision a carrier is allowed to make. It is a right to be inspected on the roof's actual condition rather than its birthday.

 A plain-language summary of the statute, with the text of the law, is available on our Florida roof age law resource page at mmroofrepair.com/florida-roof-age-law.

 Why Roof Age and Roof Condition Are Not the Same Thing

 On the Treasure Coast, most older homes carry concrete or clay tile roofs. Tile is not the waterproofing layer. The underlayment beneath the tile is.

 A 20- or 25-year-old tile roof can have tile that is largely sound and underlayment that still has service life, with failures concentrated in the places that handle the most water: valleys, perimeter edges, and flashing transitions around chimneys, walls and skylights. Those are the areas that age fastest, because that is where the water goes.

 That is why a documented tile roof inspection so often tells a different story than the installation date. In the more than 100 five-year roof certifications our company has issued since 2023, the deficiencies that put an older tile roof at risk have usually been localized and repairable, not spread evenly across the entire roof. Earlier this year we certified a 25-year-old oceanfront tile roof in Highland Beach that, by age alone, would have been scheduled for a full tear-off.

 The valleys and perimeter edges were rebuilt with new self-adhered underlayment and copper drip edge, each tile went back in its original position, and the roof was certified for more than five years of remaining life with a ten-page photographic record .

 What a Proper Roof Inspection and Five-Year Roof Certification Should Document

 Not every piece of paper called a roof certification is worth the same. A credible five-year roof certification is a licensed professional's written opinion, based on an actual inspection, and it should contain five parts:

 Findings: what the inspector observed across each roof system, including tile, flat sections, underlayment where sampled, flashing and penetrations. Deficiencies identified: active leaks, broken or loose tiles, deteriorated underlayment, damaged sheathing and flashing failures, recorded by location. Repairs performed: exactly what was corrected before the certification was signed. Remaining useful life opinion: the inspector's professional judgment, stated with its basis. Limitations: what was not inspected or tested. A certification is not a warranty, and an honest one says so. Every finding should be tied to dated photographs and the inspector's license number. If a document cannot show you where the problem was found and how it was addressed, it is an opinion without evidence, and it will not hold up when it matters.

 What to Do When the Non-Renewal Letter Arrives

 Read the letter carefully and note the deadline. Most give a defined window to respond. Ask your agent, in writing, whether the non-renewal is based on roof age, and reference Florida Statute 627.7011(5). Schedule a roof inspection with an authorized inspector, and ask up front what the written report will include and whether the inspector photographs every deficiency. If repairs are needed to reach five years of remaining life, have them completed and documented before the certification is signed. Deliver the inspection report and certification to your agent, and keep a copy with your closing documents and your wind mitigation report. Five Questions to Ask Before Signing a Roof Replacement Contract

 Has anyone inspected and photographed the roof's actual condition, or is replacement being recommended by age alone? Where exactly is the roof failing, and is the failure localized to valleys, edges and flashings, or spread across the field? Can the failing sections be rebuilt with new underlayment while the existing tile is preserved and reinstalled? Is the contractor a Florida-licensed roofing contractor, and is the license number on the proposal? Will the contractor return for annual roof inspections so the documentation stays current? When Roof Replacement Is the Right Answer

 This is not an argument against replacing roofs. Some roofs are at the end of their service life. When underlayment has failed across the field, when sheathing is deteriorated in many areas, or when the tile itself is no longer serviceable, replacement is the responsible decision and a good contractor will say so.

 The concern is the roof that gets torn off because of a date on a permit, before anyone has inspected, documented and explained its actual condition. Florida law gives homeowners the right to that inspection. The homeowners who benefit are the ones who know to ask for it.

hero.headline: Student swims from school bus in Port St. Lucie floodwater, raising safety questions
hero.teaser: A student entered deep floodwater after leaving a school bus in Port St. Lucie on Monday, prompting parents to question St. Lucie Public Schools’ decisions to open schools during s
hero.body:
A student entered deep floodwater after leaving a school bus in Port St. Lucie on Monday, prompting parents to question St. Lucie Public Schools’ decisions to open schools during severe weather and send buses into flooded streets. A viral video shows the student swimming home through the neighborhood, where the water has since receded.

 Neighbor Ariel Abel said the bus became stuck before the student stepped into the water. “We watched the school bus get stuck over in that turn area, and then we watched the kid get off, and he sunk straight into the water.” Lucinda Lopez also described the danger: “He literally almost went completely underwater,” she said.

 Parents have questioned whether students should have sheltered at school until conditions improved rather than boarding buses traveling through severely flooded streets. The county’s first flood advisory came just after 8 a.m. Monday, and the first flash flood warning was issued at 10:41 a.m. “Seeing the danger that all of the kids were put in is not okay,” Lopez said.

 St. Lucie Public Schools Superintendent Dr. Jon Prince apologized to families for the district’s response during a news conference Tuesday. “I completely understand the frustration families feel,” Prince said. “It caused a lot of stress for our families, and for that, I’m profoundly sorry.”

 Some parents remained dissatisfied with the apology and called for changes to protect students. “An apology doesn’t fix what is happening,” Abel said. Lopez emphasized safety over attendance: “We need to do better. We need to protect our kids at all costs. Missing a day or two of school is okay if it means keeping our kids safe at all costs.”

cards.headline: Port St. Lucie dialysis patient recalls canal rescue as body-camera video is released
cards.teaser: Maria Andrade-Vasquez feared she would not survive when floodwaters swept her transport van into a canal. Body-camera video released this week shows the response that brought her and the driver to safety.
cards.body:
Maria Andrade-Vasquez feared she would not survive when floodwaters swept her dialysis transport van into a Port St. Lucie canal Monday. Now recovering at home, she is recounting the rescue as police body-camera video released this week shows how an officer and firefighters helped save her. “Yes, very, very scared,” Andrade-Vasquez said, speaking through her son, Raul Morales, who translated from Spanish.

 Andrade-Vasquez was riding home from treatment when the van was swept off the road near Lakehurst Drive in the Swan Park community. Police said Officer Peterson arrived just 100 seconds after being dispatched to reports of a transport van in a canal off Southwest Hogan Street. The video shows Peterson rushing into the water and rescuing the driver before learning that Andrade-Vasquez was still trapped inside. As water surrounded the vehicle, rescuers said, the van tilted into the canal, leaving her trapped in the back.

 Police Chief Leo Niemczyk said wheelchair equipment in the van blocked Andrade-Vasquez’s escape. “She's wheelchair bound, so the equipment that came out of the back of the van was up in place blocking her in,” Niemczyk said. “They had to get her out of the wheelchair and pull her up over the equipment to get her out of the van.” Firefighters with St. Lucie County Fire District joined Peterson and worked with him to free her, according to police. Both Andrade-Vasquez and the driver were rescued safely.

 Morales said his mother still struggles to understand how rescuers freed her so quickly. “To me it was amazing to see how quick they did what they did,” he said. Andrade-Vasquez, a mother of four, grandmother of 10 and cancer survivor, remains grateful to the first responders who saved her. Morales said she is still processing the trauma of the rescue and plans to continue dialysis treatments three times a week as she recovers at home with her family.

cards.headline: Florida's Roof Age Law: The Roof Inspection Treasure Coast Homeowners Can Request Before Replacing a Roof Over 15 Years Old
cards.teaser: Under Florida Statute 627.7011, a homeowner with a roof 15 years or older can have it inspected before an insurer requires replacement. Here is what Martin and St. Lucie County homeowners should know, and what a proper roof inspection documents.
cards.body:
If you own a home in Stuart, Jensen Beach, Palm City, Port St. Lucie, Fort Pierce or anywhere along Hutchinson Island, and your roof is more than 15 years old, there is a good chance you have already received the letter. It says your homeowners insurance will not be renewed unless the roof is replaced. Many Treasure Coast homeowners assume they have two choices: pay for a new roof or lose coverage. Florida law gives them a third option, and most have never heard of it.

 What Florida's Roof Age Law Actually Says

 Florida Statute 627.7011(5), often called the Florida roof age law or the 15-year roof rule, applies to homeowners insurance policies issued or renewed on or after July 1, 2022. For a roof under 15 years old, an insurer may not refuse to issue or renew a policy solely because of the roof's age. For a roof 15 years or older, the insurer must allow the homeowner to have the roof inspected by an authorized inspector, at the homeowner's expense, before requiring replacement as a condition of coverage. If that roof inspection shows the roof has five or more years of remaining useful life, the insurer may not refuse to issue or renew the policy solely because of roof age.

 Authorized inspectors under the statute include Florida-licensed roofing contractors, home inspectors, building code inspectors, general or residential contractors, engineers and architects. The law applies to homeowners policies; it does not apply to a condominium association's master policy, and it does not override every other underwriting decision a carrier is allowed to make. It is a right to be inspected on the roof's actual condition rather than its birthday.

 A plain-language summary of the statute, with the text of the law, is available on our Florida roof age law resource page at mmroofrepair.com/florida-roof-age-law.

 Why Roof Age and Roof Condition Are Not the Same Thing

 On the Treasure Coast, most older homes carry concrete or clay tile roofs. Tile is not the waterproofing layer. The underlayment beneath the tile is.

 A 20- or 25-year-old tile roof can have tile that is largely sound and underlayment that still has service life, with failures concentrated in the places that handle the most water: valleys, perimeter edges, and flashing transitions around chimneys, walls and skylights. Those are the areas that age fastest, because that is where the water goes.

 That is why a documented tile roof inspection so often tells a different story than the installation date. In the more than 100 five-year roof certifications our company has issued since 2023, the deficiencies that put an older tile roof at risk have usually been localized and repairable, not spread evenly across the entire roof. Earlier this year we certified a 25-year-old oceanfront tile roof in Highland Beach that, by age alone, would have been scheduled for a full tear-off.

 The valleys and perimeter edges were rebuilt with new self-adhered underlayment and copper drip edge, each tile went back in its original position, and the roof was certified for more than five years of remaining life with a ten-page photographic record .

 What a Proper Roof Inspection and Five-Year Roof Certification Should Document

 Not every piece of paper called a roof certification is worth the same. A credible five-year roof certification is a licensed professional's written opinion, based on an actual inspection, and it should contain five parts:

 Findings: what the inspector observed across each roof system, including tile, flat sections, underlayment where sampled, flashing and penetrations. Deficiencies identified: active leaks, broken or loose tiles, deteriorated underlayment, damaged sheathing and flashing failures, recorded by location. Repairs performed: exactly what was corrected before the certification was signed. Remaining useful life opinion: the inspector's professional judgment, stated with its basis. Limitations: what was not inspected or tested. A certification is not a warranty, and an honest one says so. Every finding should be tied to dated photographs and the inspector's license number. If a document cannot show you where the problem was found and how it was addressed, it is an opinion without evidence, and it will not hold up when it matters.

 What to Do When the Non-Renewal Letter Arrives

 Read the letter carefully and note the deadline. Most give a defined window to respond. Ask your agent, in writing, whether the non-renewal is based on roof age, and reference Florida Statute 627.7011(5). Schedule a roof inspection with an authorized inspector, and ask up front what the written report will include and whether the inspector photographs every deficiency. If repairs are needed to reach five years of remaining life, have them completed and documented before the certification is signed. Deliver the inspection report and certification to your agent, and keep a copy with your closing documents and your wind mitigation report. Five Questions to Ask Before Signing a Roof Replacement Contract

 Has anyone inspected and photographed the roof's actual condition, or is replacement being recommended by age alone? Where exactly is the roof failing, and is the failure localized to valleys, edges and flashings, or spread across the field? Can the failing sections be rebuilt with new underlayment while the existing tile is preserved and reinstalled? Is the contractor a Florida-licensed roofing contractor, and is the license number on the proposal? Will the contractor return for annual roof inspections so the documentation stays current? When Roof Replacement Is the Right Answer

 This is not an argument against replacing roofs. Some roofs are at the end of their service life. When underlayment has failed across the field, when sheathing is deteriorated in many areas, or when the tile itself is no longer serviceable, replacement is the responsible decision and a good contractor will say so.

 The concern is the roof that gets torn off because of a date on a permit, before anyone has inspected, documented and explained its actual condition. Florida law gives homeowners the right to that inspection. The homeowners who benefit are the ones who know to ask for it.
